title: Linux & Networking Fundamentals
description: The Linux filesystem, processes and permissions, core networking concepts, and shell scripting for automation.

lessons.title: Essential Linux and the Filesystem
lessons.description: Nearly every AI system in this curriculum eventually runs on a Linux server — this is the ground floor.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Navigate a Linux filesystem confidently and explain why understanding it matters for deploying AI systems.

sections.title: 📁 The filesystem as a tree
sections.content: Linux organizes everything as a single tree rooted at `/`, with standard locations for different purposes — `/etc` for configuration, `/var/log` for logs, `/home` for user directories. Knowing this layout means you can find a service's configuration or logs without guessing, on any Linux machine you encounter, from a cheap cloud VM to a GPU server.

sections.title: ⌨️ Commands you'll use constantly
sections.content: Navigating (`cd`, `ls`, `pwd`), inspecting files (`cat`, `less`, `tail -f` for watching a live log — exactly how you'd watch a model server's logs during a deploy), and searching (`grep`, `find`) form the daily vocabulary of operating any server, including every GPU instance and Kubernetes node discussed later in this course.

sections.title: 🔗 Why this belongs in an AI curriculum
sections.content: Every model, agent, and pipeline built throughout this curriculum eventually needs to run somewhere — and 'somewhere' is almost always some flavor of Linux. This course's remaining modules (Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD, cloud providers) all assume this foundation.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
sections.content:
Here's a tiny simulated filesystem, walked and searched with the same logic `ls`, `find`, and `grep` use, to make the standard-layout idea concrete.

```python
filesystem = {
    "/etc/nginx/nginx.conf": "server { listen 80; }",
    "/etc/app/config.yaml": "log_level: INFO",
    "/var/log/app.log": "2026-01-01 12:00:00 INFO service started\n2026-01-01 12:00:05 ERROR connection refused",
    "/home/deploy/deploy.sh": "#!/bin/bash\necho deploying...",
}

def ls(prefix):
    """Lists files whose path starts with the given prefix -- like `ls` on a directory."""
    return sorted(p for p in filesystem if p.startswith(prefix))

def grep(pattern, path):
    """Finds lines in a file containing the pattern -- like `grep pattern file`."""
    return [line for line in filesystem[path].split("\n") if pattern in line]

print("ls /etc ->", ls("/etc"))
print("ls /var/log ->", ls("/var/log"))
print("grep 'ERROR' /var/log/app.log ->", grep("ERROR", "/var/log/app.log"))
```

`ls("/etc")` finds both config files without needing to know they exist in advance, purely because configuration lives under the standard `/etc` location. `grep("ERROR", ...)` pulls out exactly the one line that matters from `/var/log/app.log` — this is the same real-time triage `tail -f` combined with `grep` gives you on an actual server: knowing *where* to look (the standard layout) and *how* to search (grep) together turn an unfamiliar server into a navigable one.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Guessing at file locations instead of relying on the standard layout.** Poking around randomly for a service's config file wastes time that a quick check of `/etc/<service-name>/` would have saved — the standard layout exists precisely so you don't have to guess.

**Reading an entire large log file instead of searching or tailing it.** `cat`-ing a multi-gigabyte log file floods your terminal and tells you nothing useful — `grep` for the pattern you care about, or `tail -f` to watch new lines as they arrive.

**Treating the filesystem layout as optional trivia rather than load-bearing knowledge.** Every later module in this course — Docker, Kubernetes, CI/CD — assumes you can navigate a Linux machine comfortably; skipping this foundation makes everything after it harder than it needs to be.

questions.question: What does the Linux filesystem's standard layout (like `/etc` for config, `/var/log` for logs) provide?
options: A predictable structure that lets you find a service's configuration or logs on any Linux machine without guessing
A guarantee that no two files can ever have the same name
Automatic backup of all files to the cloud
A requirement that all files be owned by the root user
questions.explanation: The standardized directory layout is exactly what makes navigating an unfamiliar Linux server predictable rather than a guessing game.

questions.question: Why is `tail -f` a particularly useful command for operating a deployed AI service?
options: It lets you watch a log file update in real time, useful for monitoring a model server's logs during a deploy
It permanently deletes the log file being watched
It only works on files smaller than one kilobyte
It compresses log files to save disk space
questions.explanation: Watching logs live as they're written is exactly the kind of real-time visibility needed when deploying or debugging a running service.

questions.question: Why does this Linux foundation matter for the rest of this course?
options: Because Docker, Kubernetes, and cloud providers all ultimately run on Linux servers, so this foundation underlies everything that follows
Because Linux is unrelated to any cloud infrastructure covered later
Because Kubernetes replaces the need for any Linux knowledge
Because this lesson's content will never be used again in this course
questions.explanation: Every later topic in this course builds on infrastructure that is, underneath, a Linux system — making this foundational knowledge directly relevant throughout.

questions.question: In the code example, what does `ls("/etc")` return, and why?
options: Every path in the filesystem, regardless of location
Both /etc/nginx/nginx.conf and /etc/app/config.yaml, since both paths start with the '/etc' prefix
Only /var/log/app.log
Nothing, since /etc is empty
questions.explanation: `ls` filters `filesystem` for every path starting with the given prefix, and both configuration files happen to live under `/etc`, so both are returned, sorted.

questions.question: What does `grep("ERROR", "/var/log/app.log")` return in the code example?
options: Every line in the file
An empty list, since no line contains 'ERROR'
Just the line '2026-01-01 12:00:05 ERROR connection refused'
The entire nginx.conf file
questions.explanation: `grep` filters the file's lines for the substring "ERROR", and only the second line of `/var/log/app.log` contains it, so that's the single line returned.

questions.question: Why is guessing at file locations instead of relying on the standard layout flagged as a common mistake?
options: Because poking around randomly wastes time a quick check of the standard location (like /etc/<service-name>/) would have saved
Because the standard layout doesn't actually exist on real Linux systems
Because guessing is always faster than checking the standard layout
Because file locations are randomized on every Linux system
questions.explanation: The lesson's common mistakes point out that the standard layout exists precisely to avoid the time waste of guessing at where something might be.

questions.question: Why is reading an entire large log file with `cat` instead of searching or tailing it considered a mistake?
options: Because it floods your terminal with irrelevant output and tells you nothing useful, compared to grep-ing for a specific pattern or tail -f-ing new lines
Because cat cannot technically open files larger than 1KB
Because reading log files is always illegal
Because grep and tail -f are slower than cat for any file size
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that dumping a huge log file's entire contents is unhelpful compared to targeted tools like grep or tail -f that surface only what's actually relevant.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against treating the filesystem layout as optional trivia?
options: Because every later module in this course assumes comfortable navigation of a Linux machine, so skipping this foundation makes everything after it harder
Because the filesystem layout has no bearing on any later course content
Because Docker and Kubernetes eliminate the need for any filesystem knowledge
Because this lesson's content is only tested once and never used again
questions.explanation: The lesson's common mistakes emphasize that this foundational knowledge is load-bearing for Docker, Kubernetes, and CI/CD content that follows, not a skippable detail.

lessons.title: Processes, Permissions, and Users
lessons.description: Who can run what, and what happens when a program actually executes — the security and operations backbone of any server.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain the Linux permission model and how processes relate to the services you'll deploy.

sections.title: 👤 Users, groups, and permissions
sections.content: Every file has an owner, a group, and a set of read/write/execute permissions for owner, group, and everyone else. Running a production service as an unprivileged, dedicated user rather than root limits the damage a compromised process could do — a concrete implementation of the least-privilege principle the Eval & Security and Enterprise AI courses discuss at a higher level.

sections.title: ⚙️ Processes: a running program
sections.content: A process is a program currently executing, with its own memory space, and a process ID (PID) you can use to inspect or stop it (`ps`, `kill`). Every model server, API, and background worker discussed throughout the App Dev course is, at the operating system level, just a process — understanding processes demystifies what 'restart the service' actually does.

sections.title: 🔐 Why least privilege matters operationally
sections.content: A process running with more permissions than it needs is a larger attack surface if compromised — a web server that only needs to read a specific directory shouldn't run with permission to write anywhere on the filesystem. This is the same defense-in-depth thinking from the Eval & Security course, applied at the operating-system layer rather than the model or API layer.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
sections.content:
A tiny permission-check simulation shows why running as an unprivileged user actually limits what a compromised process could do.

```python
class SimulatedFile:
    def __init__(self, owner, permissions):
        self.owner = owner
        self.permissions = permissions  # e.g. {'read': ['owner', 'group'], 'write': ['owner']}

def can_access(user, is_owner, action, file):
    allowed_roles = file.permissions.get(action, [])
    if is_owner and "owner" in allowed_roles:
        return True
    if "everyone" in allowed_roles:
        return True
    return False

app_config = SimulatedFile(owner="app-service", permissions={"read": ["owner"], "write": ["owner"]})
system_passwd = SimulatedFile(owner="root", permissions={"read": ["everyone"], "write": ["owner"]})

print("unprivileged 'app-service' user reading its own config:",
      can_access("app-service", is_owner=True, action="read", file=app_config))
print("unprivileged 'app-service' user writing to system_passwd (owned by root):",
      can_access("app-service", is_owner=False, action="write", file=system_passwd))
print("a compromised root process writing to system_passwd:",
      can_access("root", is_owner=True, action="write", file=system_passwd))
```

The unprivileged `app-service` user can read and write its own config (it's the owner), but `can_access` correctly returns `False` when that same non-owner user tries to write to `system_passwd`, which only `root` (its owner) can write to. The third check shows exactly the risk the lesson describes: if the compromised process *were* running as `root`, that same write would succeed — the permission model is what turns "run as an unprivileged user" from a suggestion into an actual, enforced boundary.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Running a production service as root 'just to avoid permission errors.'** This is exactly the mistake the lesson warns about — sidestepping a permission error by running as root removes the entire protective boundary, rather than fixing the actual permission the service needs.

**Confusing killing a process with actually fixing the underlying problem.** `kill`-ing and restarting a crashing process can mask a real bug that will simply recur, rather than treating the crash as a signal to investigate.

**Granting broad, unnecessary permissions during setup 'to save time later.'** Least privilege is easiest to get right from the start; broadening access under time pressure and never narrowing it back down is how permission creep accumulates on a system.

questions.question: Why is running a production service as a dedicated, unprivileged user preferable to running it as root?
options: It limits the damage a compromised process could do, implementing least-privilege at the operating system level
It makes the service run measurably faster
Root users cannot run any services at all
Unprivileged users have unlimited filesystem access by default
questions.explanation: Restricting a process's permissions to only what it actually needs directly limits the blast radius if that process is ever compromised.

questions.question: What is a process, in Linux terms?
options: A program currently executing, with its own memory space and a process ID
A file stored permanently on disk
A network connection between two servers
A type of user account
questions.explanation: A process is the runtime instance of a running program, distinct from the static file that defines it on disk.

questions.question: How does this lesson's least-privilege principle connect to material from the Eval & Security course?
options: It applies the same defense-in-depth, least-privilege thinking at the operating-system layer instead of the model or API layer
It contradicts the security principles taught in the Eval & Security course
It has no relationship to security concepts covered elsewhere
It only applies to database security, not operating systems
questions.explanation: The recurring theme of limiting privilege to what's actually needed shows up again here, just applied to OS-level process permissions rather than model or API access.

questions.question: In the code example, why does `can_access("app-service", is_owner=False, action="write", file=system_passwd)` return False?
options: Because 'app-service' is not the owner of system_passwd, and system_passwd's write permission is restricted to its owner only
Because system_passwd has no write permission defined for anyone
Because app-service does not exist as a user
Because can_access always returns False for the write action
questions.explanation: `system_passwd.permissions["write"]` is `["owner"]`, and since `is_owner=False` for this call, the `if is_owner and "owner" in allowed_roles` check fails, and there's no "everyone" entry either, so access is correctly denied.

questions.question: What does the third `can_access` call in the code example demonstrate?
options: That root can never write to any file under any circumstances
That if the compromised process were running as root (the file's actual owner), the same write that was denied to app-service would succeed
That system_passwd cannot be written to by anyone, including root
That the permission model has no effect on root users
questions.explanation: The third call passes `"root"` with `is_owner=True`, and since root is `system_passwd`'s actual owner with write permission, `can_access` returns `True` -- illustrating exactly why running a service as root removes the protective boundary that denied the earlier, unprivileged attempt.

questions.question: Why is running a production service as root 'just to avoid permission errors' flagged as a common mistake?
options: Because it removes the entire protective boundary the permission model provides, rather than fixing the actual permission the service needs
Because permission errors are always bugs in the operating system itself
Because root users cannot run any services
Because avoiding permission errors is never possible in Linux
questions.explanation: The lesson's common mistakes identify this as sidestepping the real fix (granting the specific permission needed) by removing all restrictions instead, which defeats the purpose of least privilege.

questions.question: Why is repeatedly killing and restarting a crashing process, without investigating further, called a mistake?
options: Because it can mask a real underlying bug that will simply recur, rather than treating the crash as a signal worth investigating
Because kill and restart always permanently fixes any crash
Because processes can never be restarted once killed
Because crashing processes never have an underlying cause
questions.explanation: The lesson points out that restarting a crashing process without understanding why it crashed just delays the same problem from recurring, rather than addressing its root cause.

questions.question: Why is granting broad, unnecessary permissions during setup 'to save time later' considered a mistake?
options: Because least privilege is easiest to get right from the start, and broadened access under time pressure tends to accumulate as permission creep rather than getting narrowed back down later
Because broad permissions always cause immediate system crashes
Because Linux automatically revokes excess permissions after 24 hours
Because narrow permissions are always harder to configure than broad ones
questions.explanation: The lesson warns that permissions granted broadly under time pressure tend to stick around rather than getting revisited and tightened later, which is exactly how permission creep builds up on a system.

lessons.title: Networking Basics: IP, DNS, and Ports
lessons.description: Every API call in this curriculum — to an LLM, a vector database, or your own service — travels over this stack.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Explain what an IP address, a DNS lookup, and a port each identify in a network request.

sections.title: 📍 IP addresses: where a machine lives on the network
sections.content: An IP address identifies a specific machine (or a specific interface) on a network, the way a street address identifies a building. Every request from your API to an LLM provider, or from a client to your own deployed service, ultimately resolves to an IP address to know where to actually send the network traffic.

sections.title: 📖 DNS: translating names to addresses
sections.content: DNS (Domain Name System) translates a human-readable name like `api.openai.com` into the IP address a computer actually needs to route traffic — the same idea as a phone book, done automatically on every request so humans and applications can use memorable names instead of raw numeric addresses.

sections.title: 🚪 Ports: which service on that machine
sections.content: A single machine can run many services simultaneously — a web server, a database, an SSH daemon — each listening on a different port number, so incoming traffic on port 443 goes to the web server while traffic on port 5432 goes to the database. This is why a service's address is often written as `host:port` — both pieces are needed to reach the right service on the right machine.

sections.title: 🔗 Where this becomes concrete later
sections.content: Every load balancer, container, and Kubernetes service in this course routes traffic using exactly these three concepts — an IP, resolved from a DNS name, directed to a specific port. Understanding them here makes the later infrastructure lessons much less abstract.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
sections.content:
Here's DNS resolution and port routing simulated together, showing exactly what a request needs before it can actually reach the right service.

```python
dns_records = {"api.example.com": "203.0.113.10", "db.example.com": "203.0.113.20"}

services_by_ip_and_port = {
    ("203.0.113.10", 443): "web-api-service",
    ("203.0.113.10", 22): "ssh-daemon",
    ("203.0.113.20", 5432): "postgres-database",
}

def resolve_and_connect(hostname, port):
    ip = dns_records.get(hostname)
    if ip is None:
        return f"DNS lookup failed for {hostname!r}"
    service = services_by_ip_and_port.get((ip, port))
    if service is None:
        return f"resolved {hostname} -> {ip}, but nothing listening on port {port}"
    return f"resolved {hostname} -> {ip}, connected to {service!r} on port {port}"

print(resolve_and_connect("api.example.com", 443))
print(resolve_and_connect("api.example.com", 22))
print(resolve_and_connect("db.example.com", 5432))
print(resolve_and_connect("api.example.com", 5432))   # right host, wrong port
print(resolve_and_connect("unknown.example.com", 443))  # DNS lookup fails entirely
```

`resolve_and_connect` mirrors what happens on every real request: `dns_records.get(hostname)` is the DNS step, translating a name into an IP; `services_by_ip_and_port.get((ip, port))` is the port-routing step, since the same IP (`203.0.113.10`) hosts two entirely different services depending on which port is targeted. Requesting the right host but the wrong port (`api.example.com` on 5432) correctly finds nothing, since that IP has no service registered on 5432 — and an unknown hostname fails at the very first DNS step, before port routing is even considered.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Assuming a service is unreachable because of DNS when the real problem is the port.** "Connection refused" (wrong or closed port) and "could not resolve host" (DNS failure) are different problems with different fixes — diagnosing which one you're actually facing saves real debugging time.

**Forgetting that DNS records can be stale or cached.** A DNS change doesn't always take effect instantly everywhere — cached results from a previous lookup can point to an old IP for a while after a record is updated.

**Treating `host:port` as one opaque string instead of two separate, independently-failing pieces.** Debugging a connection problem goes faster once you check the DNS resolution and the port-level reachability as two separate questions, rather than one combined mystery.

questions.question: What does DNS translate?
options: A human-readable domain name into the IP address a computer needs to route traffic
An IP address into a MAC address
A port number into a domain name
A file path into a URL
questions.explanation: DNS resolution is exactly the name-to-address translation that lets humans use memorable names while the network still routes by IP address.

questions.question: Why can one machine run multiple network services simultaneously without conflict?
options: Each service listens on a different port number, so traffic can be directed to the correct service by port
Because only one service is ever allowed to run on a machine at a time
Because each service requires its own separate physical machine
Because IP addresses automatically change for each running service
questions.explanation: Ports provide the addressing granularity within a single machine, letting multiple services coexist and each receive their own traffic.

questions.question: Why does understanding IP, DNS, and ports make later lessons on load balancers and Kubernetes less abstract?
options: Because those systems route traffic using exactly these same concepts — an IP resolved from a DNS name, directed to a specific port
Because load balancers and Kubernetes don't use networking concepts at all
Because DNS is only relevant to email systems, not infrastructure
Because ports are unrelated to how containers communicate
questions.explanation: The infrastructure covered later in this course builds directly on these fundamental networking concepts, rather than introducing an unrelated new model.

questions.question: In the code example, what does `resolve_and_connect("api.example.com", 5432)` return, and why?
options: A successful connection to postgres-database
A message saying it resolved to the IP but nothing is listening on port 5432, since that IP only has services registered on ports 443 and 22
A DNS lookup failure
The exact same result as resolve_and_connect("db.example.com", 5432)
questions.explanation: The hostname resolves fine to `203.0.113.10`, but `services_by_ip_and_port` has no entry for `("203.0.113.10", 5432)` -- only ports 443 and 22 are registered for that IP -- so the function reports resolution succeeded but nothing is listening on that port.

questions.question: Why does `resolve_and_connect("unknown.example.com", 443)` fail differently from the previous question's example?
options: Because it fails at the DNS step itself, before port routing is ever considered, since 'unknown.example.com' has no entry in dns_records
Because port 443 doesn't exist on any machine
Because it fails at the exact same step as api.example.com on port 5432
Because unknown.example.com resolves to a different IP with no ports at all
questions.explanation: `dns_records.get("unknown.example.com")` returns `None` since that hostname isn't in the dictionary, so the function returns the DNS-failure message immediately, without ever reaching the port-lookup step -- a structurally different failure than resolving successfully but finding no service on the requested port.

questions.question: Why is assuming a service is unreachable due to DNS, when the real problem is the port, flagged as a mistake?
options: Because 'connection refused' (a port problem) and 'could not resolve host' (a DNS problem) are different failures with different fixes, so correctly diagnosing which one you're facing saves debugging time
Because DNS and ports are actually the exact same concept
Because port problems can never occur in practice
Because DNS failures and port failures always require identical fixes
questions.explanation: The lesson's common mistakes point out that these are structurally different problems, and conflating them wastes time chasing the wrong fix.

questions.question: Why is forgetting that DNS records can be stale or cached a mistake?
options: Because a DNS change doesn't always take effect instantly everywhere, so cached results from a previous lookup can point to an old IP for a while after a record is updated
Because DNS caching never actually happens on real systems
Because DNS records update instantly and globally the moment they're changed
Because cached DNS results are always more accurate than fresh lookups
questions.explanation: The lesson warns that DNS propagation isn't instantaneous, so a recently changed record might still resolve to the old IP for some clients due to caching.

questions.question: Why should `host:port` be treated as two separate, independently-failing pieces rather than one opaque string?
options: Because debugging a connection problem goes faster when DNS resolution and port-level reachability are checked as two separate questions, rather than one combined mystery
Because host and port cannot actually fail independently of each other
Because treating them separately always doubles debugging time
Because ports do not affect network routing at all
questions.explanation: The lesson's common mistakes highlight that separating the DNS question from the port question makes diagnosing a connectivity problem far more tractable than treating the whole thing as one undifferentiated failure.

lessons.title: Shell Scripting for Automation
lessons.description: The small scripts that quietly hold together every deploy pipeline you'll ever touch.

sections.title: What you should be able to do
sections.content: Write a simple shell script that automates a repeated multi-step task, and explain why automation matters operationally.

sections.title: 📜 What a shell script actually is
sections.content: A shell script is just a sequence of the same commands you'd type interactively, saved to a file and run as a unit — variables, conditionals, and loops work much like in any programming language, letting you automate a sequence like 'build the container, run the tests, push the image' as one repeatable, reliable command.

sections.title: 🔁 Why automate rather than repeat manually
sections.content: A manual, multi-step deploy process run by hand is slow and error-prone — a forgotten step, a typo, an inconsistent order between two people's manual runs. A script runs the same steps the same way every time, which is exactly the reliability property the CI/CD module later in this course builds much larger automation around.

sections.title: ⚠️ Scripts need error handling too
sections.content: A script that doesn't check whether each step actually succeeded before moving to the next can silently continue after a failure, doing more damage — `set -e` (stop on first error) and explicit checks on critical steps are the shell-script equivalent of the error-handling discipline covered throughout the App Dev course's API-building lessons.

sections.title: 💻 Seeing it in practice
sections.content:
Here's the difference `set -e`-style behavior makes, modeled in Python: a script that keeps going after a failure versus one that stops immediately.

```python
def run_step(name, succeeds):
    print(f"running: {name}")
    if not succeeds:
        print(f"  FAILED: {name}")
    return succeeds

steps = [
    ("build container", True),
    ("run tests", False),   # this step fails
    ("push image", True),   # should NEVER run after a failed test step
]

# --- Without error handling: keeps going regardless ---

print("--- no error handling ---")
for name, succeeds in steps:
    run_step(name, succeeds)
print("script finished 'successfully' even though a step failed and pushed a broken image\n")

# --- With set -e style error handling: stops at the first failure ---

print("--- with 'set -e' style error handling ---")
for name, succeeds in steps:
    ok = run_step(name, succeeds)
    if not ok:
        print(f"stopping script immediately -- '{name}' failed, later steps skipped")
        break
```

Without error handling, the loop runs all three steps regardless of outcome — including `push image`, which runs even though `run tests` just failed, exactly the silent-continue risk the lesson warns about. With the `set -e`-style check, the loop's `if not ok: break` stops execution the moment `run tests` fails, so `push image` never runs at all — a broken image never gets pushed.

sections.title: Common mistakes
sections.content:
**Writing a script with no error handling, assuming every step will always succeed.** As the code example shows, this can let a broken later step (like pushing an image) run anyway after an earlier step has already failed.

**Hardcoding values that should be parameters or environment variables.** A script with a hardcoded environment name or file path only works in the one context it was written for, defeating the reusability that makes automation valuable in the first place.

**Treating a working script as "done" with no comments or documentation.** A script that only its original author understands becomes a liability the moment that person is unavailable — a few lines explaining *why* a non-obvious step exists pays for itself quickly.

questions.question: What is a shell script, fundamentally?
options: A sequence of commands saved to a file and run as a single repeatable unit, with support for variables, conditionals, and loops
A special kind of database query language
A compiled binary that cannot be edited after creation
A configuration file with no executable logic
questions.explanation: A shell script is just ordinary interactive commands captured into a reusable, automatable sequence — not a fundamentally different kind of artifact.

questions.question: Why is a scripted deploy process more reliable than a manual, step-by-step process run by hand?
options: A script runs the same steps the same way every time, avoiding forgotten steps, typos, or inconsistencies between different people's manual runs
Scripts always run instantly with zero execution time
Manual processes are always faster than scripted ones
Scripts eliminate the need for testing entirely
questions.explanation: Consistency and repeatability are exactly what automation buys over manual execution, which is prone to human error and inconsistency.

questions.question: What does `set -e` (or similar error handling) protect a script against?
options: Silently continuing to later steps after an earlier step has already failed
Running the script faster than without it
Preventing the script from ever being edited again
Automatically fixing any bugs in the script's logic
questions.explanation: Explicit error handling ensures a failure is caught and stops execution, rather than letting the script blindly proceed and potentially cause further damage.

questions.question: In the code example, what happens to 'push image' in the 'no error handling' run, even though 'run tests' fails?
options: It's automatically skipped
It still runs, since the loop has no check that stops it after a failed step
It fails silently without printing anything
The script crashes with an exception
questions.explanation: The 'no error handling' loop calls `run_step` for every entry in `steps` unconditionally, so `push image` runs regardless of `run tests` having just failed -- exactly the silent-continue risk the lesson warns about.

questions.question: In the 'with error handling' version, what causes the loop to stop before `push image` runs?
options: The if not ok: break check, triggered when run_step returns False for the failed 'run tests' step
A random decision by the script
push image is removed from the steps list entirely
The script runs push image first, then stops
questions.explanation: When `run_step("run tests", False)` returns `False`, the `if not ok: break` check inside the loop triggers, printing the stop message and exiting the loop before `push image` is ever reached.

questions.question: Why is writing a script with no error handling, assuming every step will always succeed, flagged as a mistake?
options: Because it can let a broken later step run anyway after an earlier step has already failed, as shown in the code example
Because scripts without error handling always run faster
Because error handling is impossible to implement in shell scripts
Because every step in a script always succeeds by definition
questions.explanation: The lesson's common mistakes directly reference the code example's demonstration: without error handling, a failure doesn't stop later, potentially damaging steps from running.

questions.question: Why is hardcoding values that should be parameters or environment variables considered a mistake?
options: Because a script with a hardcoded environment name or file path only works in the one context it was written for, defeating the reusability automation is meant to provide
Because hardcoded values always run faster than parameterized ones
Because shell scripts cannot technically accept parameters
Because hardcoding values is required for security reasons
questions.explanation: The lesson explains that hardcoding undermines the very reusability that makes automation valuable — a script tied to one specific context can't be reused elsewhere without editing it.

questions.question: Why does the lesson warn against treating a working script as 'done' with no comments or documentation?
options: Because a script only its original author understands becomes a liability the moment that person is unavailable
Because comments always slow down script execution significantly
Because documented scripts cannot be version controlled
Because undocumented scripts are always more reliable
questions.explanation: The lesson points out that a few lines explaining non-obvious steps pays off quickly, since an undocumented script becomes hard to maintain or trust once the original author isn't available to explain it.
